title: Buddhist Political Thought and Social Contract

scenes.text: Can an otherworldly religion teach us how to run a government?
scenes.narration: Think about this: Buddha left his palace to seek spiritual peace, yet kings queued up for his advice on politics. Let us explore how Buddhist thought built one of history's first social contracts!

scenes.text: Choosing a team captain to stop arguments on the playground.
scenes.narration: As an everyday analogy, imagine playing cricket without an umpire when everyone fights over who owns the bat. To stop the chaos, players get together and agree to elect a fair captain.

scenes.heading: Origin of the State
scenes.narration: Here is how statehood started according to Buddhism. When private property emerged, people began fighting, so they made a contract among themselves to elect the noblest person, called Mahasammat, meaning the great chosen one.

scenes.heading: Hindu vs Buddhist Kingship
scenes.narration: Notice the big contrast! While ancient Hindu tradition saw kings as divine rulers choosing force to conquer land, Buddhism proposed a republican model where a world monarch rules through love and moral law, called Dhamma.

scenes.heading: Ashoka's Duties of a King
scenes.narration: Emperor Ashoka expanded these duties into practical statecraft. He believed a king must serve humanity, send peaceful envoys instead of invading neighbours, and protect animals from cruelty.

scenes.heading: Equality and Deliberative Democracy
scenes.narration: Buddhism did not stop at kingship; it rejected the caste system and welcomed women equally into the monastic community, called the Sangha. These assemblies practiced deliberative democracy, where members openly debated and decided policies together.

Here is your quick recap. First, the state began to protect property through human contract. Second, the ruler is an elected servant of love. Finally, the Sangha championed equality and democratic debate.
